title: Liverpool weather: sun and rain in one day, daylight vs sunshine

lines: In Liverpool, you can leave home in sunshine,
get rained on at the bus stop,
and be back in sunshine before the bus arrives.
There's a reason. Britain sits where different air masses meet.
The Met Office says the most common one arrives from the north-west:
cold polar air that warms and picks up moisture as it crosses the Atlantic.
That makes it unstable, and unstable air builds showers.
A shower is small. One can cover as little as a single square kilometre,
drifting on the wind.
So one street gets soaked while the next stays dry.
And daylight is not the same as sunshine.
Daylight is just the time between sunrise and sunset.
In late December, Liverpool gets about seven and a half hours of it. In late June, about seventeen.
Sunshine hours only count the time the sun actually shines through.
Across north-west England and north Wales, December averages about forty hours of sunshine in the whole month.
This is where one tool in our Liverpool student accommodation mini program helps.
Pick a building, open the sunlight reference, and drag through the day.
Switch between the winter and summer solstice,
and you can see where the sun sits and which outer walls face it.
It's a guide to orientation, and a starting point for asking about a specific room.
It doesn't account for neighbouring buildings, cloud, or light indoors.
The seasons explain the gap.
At midday in midwinter, the sun over Liverpool climbs only about thirteen degrees above the horizon,
so your shadow is around four times your height.
At midsummer it reaches about sixty degrees, and your shadow shrinks to just over half.
So when you check the forecast, skip the single icon for the day. Read it hour by hour.
On the Met Office forecast, a seventy percent chance means seven in ten that some rain falls within that hour,
not rain all day.
Britain has sunny days and grey days,
and quite often, both in one afternoon.
